title: Genesis 25:1–18
context: After Sarah’s death the narrator records Abraham’s later sons by Keturah, the gift of the estate to Isaac, Abraham’s death and burial by Isaac and Ishmael, God’s blessing on Isaac, and Ishmael’s twelve princes. The chapter closes Abraham’s story while distinguishing the covenant heir from other offspring.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What earlier interpreters on each side wrote about Genesis 25:1–18.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Five and thirty years Abraham lived after the marriage of Isaac, and all that is recorded concerning him during that time lies here in a very few verses: we hear no more of God's extraordinary appearances to him, or trials of him; for all the days even of the greatest saints are not eminent days, some slide on silently, and neither come nor go with observation: such were these last days of Abraham. We have here an account of his children by Keturah, another wife, which be married after the death of Sarah.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 25:1)

reformed.quote: Then again Abraham took a wife It seems very absurd that Abraham, who is said to have been dead in his own body thirty-eight years before the decease of Sarah, should, after her death, marry another wife. such an act was, certainly, unworthy of his gravity. Besides, when Paul commends his faith, ( Romans 4:19 ,) he not only asserts that the womb of Sarah was dead, when Isaac was about to be born, but also that the body of the father himself was dead.

verses.text: Abraham took another wife, and her name was Keturah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Keturah is named as wife. Abraham’s household is larger than Isaac; later verse 6 will group her sons with the sons of Abraham’s concubines.

Arminian readers honor this marriage and children. God’s particular covenant with Isaac does not make other sons fictional or unloved.
verses.reformedNotes:
After Sarah, Abraham takes Keturah. The genealogy is history, not a detour from the promise.

Reformed readers already know Isaac is the sworn seed (Gen 17; 21). Other sons will be listed as gift, not as rivals to the oath.

verses.text: She bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Six named sons, including Midian, who will matter later in Israel’s story. These are Abraham’s offspring in the ordinary sense.

God can be kind to many children of Abraham without collapsing the covenant into a single household.
verses.reformedNotes:
Keturah’s sons are named one by one, Midian among them. The line of promise is not the only line that exists.

God records them because they are true, then will distinguish Isaac’s inheritance. Election of the seed does not erase neighbors on the family tree.

verses.text: Jokshan became the father of Sheba, and Dedan. The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim.
verses.arminianNotes:
Grandsons and tribal names appear. Abraham’s fruitfulness through Keturah spreads into peoples.

Arminians hear sincere kindness granted beyond the covenant heir—nations, names, not a polite fiction.
verses.reformedNotes:
Sheba, Dedan, and Dedan’s clans are mapped. Providence writes extra-covenant peoples into Abraham’s story.

The narrator can honor these tribes without making them the seed of promise.

verses.text: The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the children of Keturah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Midian’s sons are listed; “all these were the children of Keturah” closes the branch.

Arminians refuse to treat them as a footnote of shame. They are Abraham’s children, even if they are not Isaac.
verses.reformedNotes:
The summary gathers Keturah’s children as a completed set.

They belong to Abraham’s house historically; they will not inherit the sworn estate. The next verses make the distinction without contempt.

verses.text: Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac,
verses.arminianNotes:
The estate goes to Isaac. Covenant particularity is not in doubt: the heir is named, not guessed.

Arminians typically add that this choice does not cancel kindness to other sons. God’s particular gift of the promise-line is compatible with sincere generosity elsewhere.
verses.reformedNotes:
“All that he had” to Isaac is the legal and theological point. The line of promise receives the inheritance by Abraham’s act under God’s purpose.

Reformed readers hear election of the seed taking household form: Isaac, not a committee of sons, is heir.
verses.keyContrast: Both take Isaac as the covenant heir, not a random favorite. Arminians stress that this particular choice sits beside gifts and kept promises to other sons; Reformed readers press God’s free purpose in electing the line of promise, so the estate follows the sworn seed.

verses.text: but Abraham gave gifts to the sons of Abraham’s concubines. While he still lived, he sent them away from Isaac his son, eastward, to the east country.
verses.arminianNotes:
Gifts, not the estate; sent east while Abraham still lives, so Isaac is not crowded out. Kindness is true; distinction is no illusion.

The verse presses a father who keeps the promise to Isaac without leaving the others empty-handed. Particular election of the heir does not erase provision.
verses.reformedNotes:
Gifts versus “all that he had”: the sons of the concubines are provided for and sent away from Isaac.

They are not nothing, and they are not the covenant seed. Eastward removal protects the heir God named.
verses.keyContrast: Shared ground: gifts are true and Isaac remains sole heir. Arminians typically stress sincere kindness that is not erased by the particular choice of Isaac; Reformed readers commonly stress that provision differs from being the promised seed.

verses.text: These are the days of the years of Abraham’s life which he lived: one hundred seventy-five years.
verses.arminianNotes:
A numbered life: 175 years. The pilgrim’s days are counted as gift.

In practice: long years under promise invite gratitude and continued trust, not a claim that Abraham earned the span.
verses.reformedNotes:
One hundred seventy-five years are the Lord’s numbering.

The friend of God dies on a timetable God wrote. The days of his years are providence, not luck.

verses.text: Abraham gave up his spirit, and died at a good old age, an old man, and full of years, and was gathered to his people.
verses.arminianNotes:
Good old age, full of years, gathered to his people—death as completion, not defeat.

The passage carries a kept word: God walked with him to the end. Fullness is gift received along a life of faith.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Gathered to his people” looks beyond the cave. The man of the covenant dies full, under the God who called him.

A good old age is the Lord’s finishing of a life He began (Gen 12).

verses.text: Isaac and Ishmael, his sons, buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron, the son of Zohar the Hittite, which is near Mamre,
verses.arminianNotes:
Both sons bury him. Rivalry is not the last word at the grave.

Isaac the heir and Ishmael the sent-away son can still honor their father together. Grace does not require erasing Ishmael from the funeral.
verses.reformedNotes:
Isaac and Ishmael stand at Machpelah, the purchased cave. The heir and the other son share grief.

Providence can reunite them for burial without rewriting who carries the promise.

verses.text: the field which Abraham purchased from the children of Heth. Abraham was buried there with Sarah, his wife.
verses.arminianNotes:
The first plot in Canaan holds husband and wife.

Arminians hear faith’s foothold kept: what he bought in chapter 23 is where he now lies. Promise still waits for more land, but this grave is historical.
verses.reformedNotes:
Title from the Hittites, burial with Sarah. The sworn couple rest in the only acre they legally held.

God kept a burying place. The covenant pair lie together under a deed, awaiting a larger possession.

verses.text: After the death of Abraham, God blessed Isaac, his son. Isaac lived by Beer Lahai Roi.
verses.arminianNotes:
God blesses Isaac after Abraham’s death—the promise does not die with the patriarch. He settles at Beer-lahai-roi, already marked by God’s seeing (Gen 16).

Blessing is God’s ongoing, sincere action toward the heir, to be received in faith.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator names the Giver: God blessed Isaac. The seed line continues by divine act, not by Abraham’s remaining strength.

Election of Isaac is confirmed in blessing after the father’s death. Beer-lahai-roi is where he dwells under that word.

verses.text: Now this is the history of the generations of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s servant, bore to Abraham.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ishmael gets a toledoth. He is Abraham’s son, Hagar’s child, named without sneer.

The covenant heir is Isaac, and Ishmael is still Abraham’s son. God can keep a particular promise without deleting this heading.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Generations of Ishmael” is history under God’s providence. Parentage is stated: Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s servant.

The narrator honors the line, then will show twelve princes—fulfillment of Gen 17:20, not a rival to Isaac’s oath.

verses.text: These are the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their names, according to the order of their birth: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,
verses.arminianNotes:
Birth-order names begin. Firstborn Nebaioth, then Kedar and the rest.

God attends to Ishmael’s household with the same narrative care He gives other families. Kindness named in order is not a slip.
verses.reformedNotes:
Ishmael’s sons are listed in order, with the firstborn named first. These sons exist because God said Ishmael would live and become a nation (Gen 17:20; 21:13).

Particular election of Isaac never meant Ishmael would be childless.

verses.arminianNotes:
Three more of Ishmael’s sons are named. Even a short verse is a record of kept life.

Arminians hear God remembering people who will not carry the covenant seed. They are not invisible to Him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Mishma, Dumah, Massa stand in the list God wanted written.

Reformed comfort from another angle: providence is detailed. The God who elects Isaac still numbers Ishmael’s sons.

verses.text: Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.
verses.arminianNotes:
The list completes toward twelve.

The count is heading toward the “twelve princes” of verse 16—a promise sincerely kept (Gen 17:20), not a consolation prize spoken in bad faith.
verses.reformedNotes:
Five more names finish the roster.

God fulfills what He said about Ishmael in particular. The same Lord who chose Isaac keeps His word to Hagar’s son.

verses.text: These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, by their villages, and by their encampments: twelve princes, according to their nations.
verses.arminianNotes:
Twelve princes—the exact shape of Genesis 17:20. Villages and encampments: settled and nomad life.

Arminians press the point: God’s particular choice of Isaac did not make this promise insincere. He said twelve princes; here they are.
verses.reformedNotes:
Twelve princes, according to their nations fulfill the word spoken over Ishmael.

Common and particular mercies can sit together. Ishmael is blessed as promised; he is still not the covenant seed through whom the nations are blessed.

verses.text: These are the years of the life of Ishmael: one hundred thirty-seven years. He gave up his spirit and died, and was gathered to his people.
verses.arminianNotes:
One hundred thirty-seven years, last breath, gathered to his people—the same death-formula used for Abraham.

Ishmael’s life is honored as a completed span under God. Gathering is not reserved for Isaac alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Ishmael’s years and gathering are recorded like a patriarch’s.

Death under providence, a people of his own. The narrator can grant him this dignity without transferring Isaac’s blessing.

verses.text: They lived from Havilah to Shur that is before Egypt, as you go toward Assyria. He lived opposite all his relatives.
verses.arminianNotes:
Geography of Ishmael’s line: Havilah to Shur, toward Assyria, “lived opposite” his kinsmen—near, not absorbed.

Arminians hear a kept place in the world beside Isaac’s house. Proximity without merger is still a kind of mercy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Settlement from Havilah to Shur fulfills the earlier word that Ishmael would dwell over against his kinsmen (cf. Gen 16:12).

God assigns a range and a posture. The cousin-nations exist by His map, beside the heir, not instead of him.
